claim: SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that is a major constituent of postsynaptic densities (PSDs) from mammalian forebrain.
source: SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that is a major constituent of postsynaptic densities (PSDs) from mammalian forebrain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The α1 isoform of synGAP binds to all three PDZ (PSD-95, Discs-large, ZO-1) domains of PSD-95.
source: Its α1 isoform binds to all three PDZ (PSD-95, Discs-large, ZO-1) domains of PSD-95, the principal PSD scaffold
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3A.

claim: SynGAP-α1 can occupy as many as 15% of the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: Its α1 isoform binds to all three PDZ (PSD-95, Discs-large, ZO-1) domains of PSD-95, the principal PSD scaffold, and can occupy as many as 15% of these PDZ domains.
evidence: This is calculated based on the relative abundance of synGAP-α1 and PSD-95 in the PSD as described in the Introduction.

claim: Phosphorylation by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) decreases synGAP-α1's affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold.
source: We show that phosphorylation by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) and Polo-like kinase-2 (PLK2) decreases its affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 3A, 3D, 7A and Table 1, showing approximately 10-fold reduction in affinity.

claim: Phosphorylation by Polo-like kinase-2 (PLK2) decreases synGAP-α1's affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold.
source: We show that phosphorylation by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) and Polo-like kinase-2 (PLK2) decreases its affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3E, showing approximately 40% reduction in binding.

claim: Three critical postsynaptic signaling proteins that bind to the PDZ domains of PSD-95 are present in higher concentration in PSDs isolated from mice with a heterozygous deletion of synGAP.
source: Finally, we show that three critical postsynaptic signaling proteins that bind to the PDZ domains of PSD-95 are present in higher concentration in PSDs isolated from mice with a heterozygous deletion of synGAP.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11, showing increased TARPs, LRRTM2, and neuroligin-2 in Syngap+/- mice.

claim: AMPARs become immobilized at the postsynaptic membrane by a three stage process involving insertion of receptors into the perisynaptic membrane, diffusion into the synapse and 'trapping' within the structure of the postsynaptic density (PSD).
source: Numerous experiments have shown that AMPARs become immobilized at the postsynaptic membrane by a three stage process involving insertion of receptors into the perisynaptic membrane, diffusion into the synapse and 'trapping' within the structure of the postsynaptic density (PSD; Opazo and Choquet, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Opazo and Choquet, 2011.

claim: The sites at which AMPARs are trapped have been referred to as 'slots'.
source: The sites at which the receptors are trapped have been referred to as 'slots,' (Shi et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shi et al., 2001.

claim: AMPAR trapping slots are believed to consist principally of PDZ domains on PSD-95.
source: The sites at which the receptors are trapped have been referred to as 'slots,' (Shi et al., 2001) and they are believed to consist principally of PDZ domains on PSD-95 (Opazo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Opazo et al., 2012.

claim: Phosphorylation by CaMKII of TARPs increases their affinity for PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: Phosphorylation by CaMKII of TARPs (Transmembrane AMPAR Regulatory Proteins; Bredt and Nicoll, 2003) increases their affinity for PDZ domains of PSD-95 suggesting that the phosphorylation may promote trapping of new AMPARs in the PSD (Tomita et al., 2005; Opazo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomita et al., 2005 and Opazo et al., 2010.

claim: The PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
source: Indeed the PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins (Figures 1 and 2B); including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs; Kornau et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kornau et al., 1995 and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2B.

claim: The PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for neuroligins.
source: Indeed the PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins (Figures 1 and 2B); including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs; Kornau et al., 1995), as well as neuroligins (Varoqueaux et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varoqueaux et al., 2006 and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2B.

claim: The PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for LRRTMs (Leucine Rich Repeat TransMembrane proteins).
source: Indeed the PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins (Figures 1 and 2B); including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs; Kornau et al., 1995), as well as neuroligins (Varoqueaux et al., 2006) and LRRTMs (Leucine Rich Repeat TransMembrane proteins; Linhoff et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Linhoff et al., 2009 and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2B.

claim: Neuroligins and LRRTMs nucleate new synapse formation and contribute to clustering of AMPARs.
source: as well as neuroligins (Varoqueaux et al., 2006) and LRRTMs (Leucine Rich Repeat TransMembrane proteins; Linhoff et al., 2009), which nucleate new synapse formation and contribute to clustering of AMPARs (Siddiqui et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Varoqueaux et al., 2006, Linhoff et al., 2009, and Siddiqui et al., 2010.

claim: AMPARs, NMDARs, TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligins comprise the most highly enriched transmembrane proteins precipitated together with PSD-95 from the PSD fraction of mouse forebrain.
source: AMPARs, NMDARs, TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligins comprise the most highly enriched transmembrane proteins precipitated together with PSD-95 from the PSD fraction of mouse forebrain (Dosemeci et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dosemeci et al., 2007.

claim: SynGAP-α1 contains a PDZ-domain ligand and binds to all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: One prominent alternatively spliced isoform, synGAP-α1 (Li et al., 2001) contains a PDZ-domain ligand and binds to all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Kim et al., 1998; Figures 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2001 and Kim et al., 1998, and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Phosphorylation by CaMKII on several sites in the regulatory region of synGAP-α1 reduces the affinity of synGAP-α1's PDZ-ligand for the three PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: We support this hypothesis by showing that phosphorylation by at least two protein kinases on several sites in the regulatory region of synGAP-α1 reduces the affinity of synGAP-α1's PDZ-ligand for the three PDZ domains of PSD-95. One of these protein kinases is CaMKII, which is activated when synaptic plasticity is initiated by activation of NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 3, 6, and 7.

claim: PLK2 is a constitutively active kinase that is induced by neuronal activity and mediates homeostatic scaling.
source: The other is PLK2, a constitutively active kinase that is induced by neuronal activity and mediates homeostatic scaling (Seeburg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seeburg et al., 2005.

claim: Binding of Ca2+/CaM to synGAP-α1 selectively reduces its affinity for PDZ3 of PSD-95.
source: We further show that binding of Ca2+/CaM to synGAP-α1 selectively reduces its affinity for PDZ3 of PSD-95.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 10A.

claim: Reduction of the total amount of synGAP in heterozygous knockout mice alters the composition of PSDs in the mutant mice.
source: Finally, we show that reduction of the total amount of synGAP in heterozygous knockout mice alters the composition of PSDs in the mutant mice in a way that is most directly explained by reduced competition from synGAP-α1 for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11.

claim: An average PSD (~360 nm in diameter) is estimated to contain ~300 molecules of PSD-95 with 900 PDZ domains.
source: An average PSD (~360 nm in diameter) is estimated to contain ~300 molecules of PSD-95 with 900 PDZ domains (Chen et al., 2005; Sugiyama et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005 and Sugiyama et al., 2005.

claim: SynGAP is nearly as abundant in the PSD as PSD-95 itself.
source: SynGAP is nearly as abundant in the PSD as PSD-95 itself (Chen et al., 1998; Cheng et al., 2006; Dosemeci et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 1998, Cheng et al., 2006, and Dosemeci et al., 2007.

claim: SynGAP is expressed as several isoforms with four different C-termini, α1, α2, β, and γ.
source: It is expressed as several isoforms with four different C-termini, α1, α2, β, and γ (Li et al., 2001; McMahon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2001 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The α1-containing isoforms are abundantly expressed at synapses and contain the PDZ ligand.
source: The α1-containing isoforms are abundantly expressed at synapses and contain the PDZ ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by the experimental data showing binding to PDZ domains.

claim: Assuming that α1 isoforms make up 30–50% of the total synaptic synGAP, synGAP-α1 could occupy 10–15% of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 in an average PSD.
source: Assuming that α1 isoforms make up 30–50% of the total synaptic synGAP, and that one synGAP-α1 molecule can bind to any one of the three PDZ domains in each molecule of PSD-95, synGAP-α1 could occupy 10–15% of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 in an average PSD.
evidence: This is calculated based on the relative abundance of synGAP and PSD-95 in the PSD.

claim: PDZ domains act as flexible protein interaction points that can be modified to support changes in cytoplasmic organization.
source: It has been proposed that, in general, PDZ domains act as flexible protein interaction points that can be modified to support changes in cytoplasmic organization (Kurakin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kurakin et al., 2007.

claim: PSD-95 protein complexes exist in dynamic equilibrium permitting continual turnover and potential rearrangement of their composition.
source: Evidence has indicated that PSD-95 protein complexes exist in dynamic equilibrium permitting continual turnover and potential rearrangement of their composition (Sturgill et al., 2009; Schapitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sturgill et al., 2009 and Schapitz et al., 2010.

claim: Phosphorylation by CaMKII triggers movement of synGAP away from the PSD in living neurons.
source: For example, two other groups used imaging to show that phosphorylation by CaMKII in living neurons triggers movement of synGAP away from the PSD (Yang et al., 2013; Araki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2013 and Araki et al., 2015.

claim: Activation of NMDARs and CaMKII causes dispersal of synGAP away from the PSD within a few minutes.
source: Activation of NMDARs and CaMKII causes dispersal of synGAP away from the PSD within a few minutes (Yang et al., 2013; Araki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2013 and Araki et al., 2015.

claim: Activation of NMDARs and CaMKII produces an equally rapid increase in the rate of trapping of AMPARs at synaptic sites.
source: The same stimuli produce an equally rapid increase in the rate of trapping of AMPARs at synaptic sites (Makino and Malinow, 2009; Opazo et al., 2010; Opazo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Makino and Malinow, 2009, Opazo et al., 2010, and Opazo et al., 2012.

claim: Increased exocytosis of AMPARs does not contribute to their increased trapping in the minutes following synaptic stimulation.
source: However, experiments show that increased exocytosis of AMPARs does not contribute to their increased trapping in the minutes following synaptic stimulation (Makino and Malinow, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makino and Malinow, 2009.

claim: Absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to accelerated ('precocious') maturation of spines.
source: An additional example of a previous result that is explained by this model, is the observation that absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to accelerated ('precocious') maturation of spines, including early movement of PSD-95 into spine heads, and ultimately larger clusters of PSD-95 in individual synapses compared to wt neurons (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Expression of wt-synGAP-α1 in synGAP KO neurons rescued all of the phenotypes of precocious spine maturation.
source: In this study, expression of wt-synGAP-α1 in the mutant neurons rescued all of these phenotypes
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Expression of synGAP-α1 with a deletion of the five residue PDZ ligand (ΔSXV) failed to rescue any of the effects of synGAP deficiency on precocious maturation of spines.
source: however, expression of synGAP-α1 with a deletion of the five residue PDZ ligand (ΔSXV) failed to rescue any of the effects of synGAP deficiency on precocious maturation of spines.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Expression of synGAPΔSXV caused an increase in the size of clusters of PSD-95 in spines compared to wt neurons.
source: In fact, expression of synGAPΔSXV caused an increase in the size of clusters of PSD-95 in spines compared to wt neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: The α1 and α2 isoforms have markedly different effects on synaptic strength when expressed in primary cultures of forebrain neurons.
source: Yet another result supporting the model is the finding of McMahon et al. (2012) that the α1 and α2 isoforms have markedly different effects on synaptic strength when expressed in primary cultures of forebrain neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: 12 to 36 hr after transfection of neurons with the A1α1 isoform of synGAP, 73% of the neurons were 'silent', compared with 11% of control neurons.
source: For example, 12 to 36 hr after transfection of the neurons with the A1α1 isoform of synGAP, 73% of the neurons were 'silent', that is, had no miniature end-plate potentials (mEPSCs), compared with 11% of control neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: Transfection with the A1α2 isoform had no effect on the proportion of silent neurons, which remained at 11%.
source: In contrast, transfection with the A1α2 isoform, which differs from α1 only in its C-terminal 48 residues and lacks a PDZ ligand, had no effect on the proportion of silent neurons, which remained at 11%.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: Neurons cultured from synGAP deficient mice have a higher average number of AMPARs at their synapses than wt neurons.
source: Neurons cultured from synGAP deficient mice have been reported by several groups to have a higher average number of AMPARs at their synapses than wt neurons (Kim et al., 2003; Vazquez et al., 2004; Rumbaugh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2003, Vazquez et al., 2004, and Rumbaugh et al., 2006.

claim: Mutations in a single copy of synGAP have been causally implicated in sporadic cases of non-syndromic ID, often associated with either autism (ASD) or epilepsy.
source: Mutations in a single copy of synGAP have been causally implicated in sporadic cases of non-syndromic ID, often associated with either autism (ASD) or epilepsy (Berryer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berryer et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations causing SynGAP haploinsufficiency appear to account for 2–9% of sporadic cases of developmental ID.
source: Although data is still sparse, mutations causing SynGAP haploinsufficiency appear to account for 2–9% of sporadic cases (Hamdan et al., 2011; Berryer et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hamdan et al., 2011 and Berryer et al., 2013.

claim: The amount of synGAP in the brains of mice with synGAP haploinsufficiency is reduced by 50%.
source: The amount of synGAP in the brains of mice with synGAP haploinsufficiency is reduced by 50% (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Phosphorylation by CaMKII reduces binding of r-synGAP-α1 to all of the individual PDZ domains and to PDZ12 and PDZ123.
source: Phosphorylation by CaMKII reduces binding of r-synGAP-α1 to all of the individual PDZ domains and to PDZ12 and PDZ123 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3A.

claim: The reduction in binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains requires the presence of both Ca2+/CaM and CaMKII in the phosphorylation reaction mixture.
source: The reduction in binding requires the presence of both Ca2+/CaM and CaMKII in the phosphorylation reaction mixture (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B.

claim: As many as 10 sites on r-synGAP-α1 are phosphorylated by CaMKII.
source: We have shown previously that as many as 10 sites on r-synGAP-α1 are phosphorylated by CaMKII (Walkup et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkup et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 5 sites on r-synGAP-α1, including site S1123, are fully phosphorylated after a 0.5 min reaction with CaMKII.
source: Approximately 5 of these, including site S1123, are fully phosphorylated after an 0.5 min reaction (Walkup et al., 2015 and Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkup et al., 2015 and demonstrated in Figure 3C.

claim: The reduction in binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123 is maximal after 0.5 min of phosphorylation by CaMKII.
source: The reduction in binding is maximal after 0.5 min, indicating that phosphorylation of the more rapidly phosphorylated sites is sufficient for full reduction of affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3D.

claim: R-synGAP-α1 can be phosphorylated by CDK5 and by PLK2.
source: R-synGAP-α1 can also be phosphorylated by CDK5 (Walkup et al., 2015) and by PLK2 (Lee et al., 2011) both of which increase its RasGAP activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walkup et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2011.

claim: Phosphorylation by CDK5 had no significant effect on affinity of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123.
source: Phosphorylation by CDK5 had no significant effect on affinity
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3E.

claim: Phosphorylation by PLK2 decreased affinity of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123 by ~40%.
source: whereas, phosphorylation by PLK2 decreased its affinity by ~40%, less strongly than does phosphorylation by CaMKII (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3E.

claim: Both CaMKII and PLK2 can phosphorylate several sites in a region marked MPD (multiple-phosphorylation domain) in Figure 2A, including serines at 808, 810, 821, 825, and 827.
source: Both CaMKII and PLK2 can phosphorylate several sites in a region marked MPD (multiple-phosphorylation domain) in Figure 2A, including serines at 808, 810, 821, 825, and 827 (Walkup et al., 2015; Walkup et al., in preperation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkup et al., 2015 and Walkup et al., in preparation, and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ1 is 220 ± 30 nM.
source: A KD of 220 ± 30 nM (Table 1) was calculated as described under Materials and methods (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is measured by SPR competition assay as shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ2 is 1500 ± 100 nM.
source: We used the same method to measure KDs for PDZ2 and PDZ3 (Figure 5A and B, respectively).
evidence: This is measured by SPR competition assay as shown in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ3 is 620 ± 70 nM.
source: We used the same method to measure KDs for PDZ2 and PDZ3 (Figure 5A and B, respectively).
evidence: This is measured by SPR competition assay as shown in Figure 5B and Table 1.

claim: The KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ12 is 350 ± 40 nM.
source: Because, PDZ12 and PDZ123 contain more than a single PDZ domain binding site, all of which have similar affinities, we determined single 'apparent' equilibrium dissociation constants (KDapp) for these two constructs.
evidence: This is measured by SPR competition assay as shown in Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: The KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123 is 4.7 ± 0.6 nM.
source: Because, PDZ12 and PDZ123 contain more than a single PDZ domain binding site, all of which have similar affinities, we determined single 'apparent' equilibrium dissociation constants (KDapp) for these two constructs.
evidence: This is measured by SPR competition assay as shown in Figure 5D and Table 1.

claim: Under these conditions, PDZ1 has a higher affinity for r-synGAP-α1 than does PDZ3.
source: These data show that, under these conditions, PDZ1 has a higher affinity for r-synGAP-α1 than does PDZ3.
evidence: This is inferred from the KD values measured by SPR and shown in Table 1.

claim: Single or multiple mutations of serines to alanine at sites S1093, S1123, or S1283 did not significantly alter binding of unphosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123.
source: Single or multiple mutations of the indicated serines to alanine did not significantly alter binding before phosphorylation
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Mutations in which site S1283 was mutated to the phosphomimetic aspartate (S1283D and S1093D/S1123D/S1283D) decreased binding of unphosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123.
source: Only mutations in which site S1283 was mutated to the phosphomimetic aspartate (S1283D and S1093D/S1123D/S1283D) decreased binding of unphosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123 with a significant p-value (p<0.0001 for both).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Phosphorylation of S1283 has the most potent effect of all the sites on binding to PDZ domains.
source: This result suggests that phosphorylation of S1283 has the most potent effect of all the sites on binding to PDZ domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The triple mutant S1093A/S1123A/S1283A was the only S to A mutation that significantly interfered with the loss of binding compared to wild type after 0.5 min of phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, the triple mutant S1093A/S1123A/S1283A was the only S to A mutation that significantly interfered with the loss of binding (p=0.0074) compared to wild type after 0.5 min of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Sites S1123 and S1283 both contribute to reduction of binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains after brief phosphorylation.
source: This result reinforces the conclusion that sites S1123 and S1283 both contribute to reduction of binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains after brief phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: None of the mutations interfere with the loss of binding to PDZ domains after ten min of phosphorylation.
source: Notably, none of the mutations interfere with the loss of binding to PDZ domains after ten min of phosphorylation (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Phosphorylation for 10 min by CaMKII increases the KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123 approximately ten-fold.
source: Phosphorylation for 10 min by CaMKII increases the KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 approximately ten-fold (Figure 7A, Table 1)
evidence: This is measured by SPR competition assay as shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: Mutation of S1283 to aspartate increases the KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123 approximately four-fold.
source: whereas mutation of S1283 to aspartate increases the KDapp approximately four-fold (Figure 7B, Table 1).
evidence: This is measured by SPR competition assay as shown in Figure 7B and Table 1.

claim: The presence of Ca2+/CaM in reactions with either CDK5/p35 or CDK5/p25 doubled the rate and stoichiometry of the phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1.
source: While studying phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1 by CDK5 (Walkup et al., 2015), we found that the presence of Ca2+/CaM in reactions with either CDK5/p35 or CDK5/p25 doubled the rate and stoichiometry of the phosphorylation (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Inclusion of Ca2+ or CaM alone in the phosphorylation reactions did not alter the rates or stoichiometry of r-synGAP-α1 phosphorylation by CDK5.
source: Inclusion of Ca2+ or CaM alone in the phosphorylation reactions did not alter the rates or stoichiometry.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Ca2+/CaM binds directly to r-synGAP-α1, causing a substrate-directed enhancement of its phosphorylation by CDK5.
source: This result suggests that Ca2+/CaM binds directly to r-synGAP-α1, causing a substrate-directed enhancement of its phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Ca2+/CaM on phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1 versus histone H1 by CDK5.

claim: R-synGAP-α1 binds to a CaM-Sepharose affinity resin in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: To further verify that Ca2+/CaM binds directly to r-synGAP-α1, we showed that r-synGAP-α1 binds to a CaM-Sepharose affinity resin in a Ca2+-dependent manner, as would be expected if it binds Ca2+/CaM specifically and with significant affinity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of Ca2+/CaM alone in a Ras- or Rap-GAP assay has no effect on the GAP activity of r-synGAP-α1.
source: We found that the presence of Ca2+/CaM alone in a Ras- or Rap-GAP assay has no effect on the GAP activity of r-synGAP-α1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for Ca2+/CaM is 9 ± 1 nM as measured by SPR.
source: Analysis of the equilibrium phase of association at each concentration (Figure 9B) yielded a KD of 9 ± 1 nM, indicative of high affinity binding.
evidence: This is measured by SPR as shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for Ca2+/CaM is 31 ± 3 nM as measured by CaM-Sepharose bead-binding assay.
source: The data were fit to hyperbolic curves and the KD's for binding of r-synGAP-α1 and sr-synGAP to Ca2+/CaM were calculated to be 31 ± 3 nM and 210 ± 30 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is measured by CaM-Sepharose bead-binding assay as shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The KD of sr-synGAP for Ca2+/CaM is 210 ± 30 nM as measured by CaM-Sepharose bead-binding assay.
source: The data were fit to hyperbolic curves and the KD's for binding of r-synGAP-α1 and sr-synGAP to Ca2+/CaM were calculated to be 31 ± 3 nM and 210 ± 30 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is measured by CaM-Sepharose bead-binding assay as shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The high affinity Ca2+/CaM binding site appears to be located in the regulatory disordered region of r-synGAP-α1, which is missing in sr-synGAP.
source: Thus, the high affinity site appears to be located in the regulatory disordered region of r-synGAP-α1, which is missing in sr-synGAP.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in KD values between r-synGAP-α1 and sr-synGAP for Ca2+/CaM.

claim: The presence of Ca2+/CaM during incubation with resin significantly reduces binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ3 and to PDZ123, but not to PDZ1 and/or PDZ2.
source: The presence of Ca2+/CaM during incubation with resin significantly reduces binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ3 and to PDZ123, but not to PDZ1 and/or PDZ2.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 10A.

claim: The effects of phosphorylation and of the presence of Ca2+/CaM during incubation with resin are not additive.
source: The effects of phosphorylation and of the presence of Ca2+/CaM during incubation with resin are not additive (Figure 10B)
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 10B.

claim: The level of synGAP is decreased in relation to PSD-95 by ~ 24% in PSDs from the Syngap+/- mice.
source: As predicted, the level of synGAP is decreased in relation to PSD-95 by ~ 24% in PSDs (p=0.0007, d = 1.75) from the Syngap+/- mice (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11A.

claim: The ratios of TARPs 2,3,4,ɣ8 to PSD-95 are significantly increased (~12%) in PSDs from Syngap+/- mice.
source: Furthermore, the ratios of TARPs 2,3,4,ɣ8, and of LRRTM2 to PSD-95 are significantly increased (Figure 11B,C; TARP/PSD-95, ~12%, p=0.017, d = 0.93
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11B.

claim: The ratio of LRRTM2 to PSD-95 is significantly increased (~14%) in PSDs from Syngap+/- mice.
source: Furthermore, the ratios of TARPs 2,3,4,ɣ8, and of LRRTM2 to PSD-95 are significantly increased (Figure 11B,C; TARP/PSD-95, ~12%, p=0.017, d = 0.93; LRRTM2/PSD-95, ~14%, p=0.0035, d = 0.66).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11C.

claim: The ratio of neuroligin-1 to PSD-95 is unchanged in the Syngap+/- mice.
source: Interestingly, the ratio of neuroligin-1 to PSD-95 is unchanged in the Syngap+/- mice (d = 0.07, Figure 11D)
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11D.

claim: The ratio of neuroligin-2 to PSD-95 is increased by ~9% in PSDs from Syngap+/- mice.
source: However, the ratio of neuroligin-2 to PSD-95 (Figure 11E) is increased by ~9% (p=0.019, d = 0.64).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11E.

claim: Neuroligin-2 normally associates mostly with inhibitory synapses and mediates their maturation.
source: Neuroligin-2 normally associates mostly with inhibitory synapses and mediates their maturation (Varoqueaux et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varoqueaux et al., 2004.

claim: Over-expression of PSD-95 in neurons causes a redistribution of neuroligin-2, increasing the proportion associated with excitatory synapses.
source: However, Levinson et al. (2005) reported that over-expression of PSD-95 in neurons causes a redistribution of neuroligin-2, increasing the proportion associated with excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levinson et al., 2005.

claim: SynGAP begins to be expressed at birth in the mouse brain and its expression increases rapidly as synapses are forming during the first weeks after birth.
source: In the mouse brain, synGAP begins to be expressed at birth and its expression increases rapidly as synapses are forming during the first weeks after birth (Vazquez et al., 2004; Barnett et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and Barnett et al., 2006.

claim: Newborns with complete deletion of Syngap appear normal, but die a few days after birth with movement defects and apparent seizure activity.
source: Newborns with complete deletion of Syngap appear normal, but die a few days after birth with movement defects and apparent seizure activity, indicating a defect as synapses are forming (Kim et al., 2003; Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2003 and Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Syngap heterozygous mice appear normal and survive into adulthood with no apparent alterations in gross brain morphology, but with defects in behavior and synaptic plasticity.
source: Syngap heterozygous mice also appear normal and survive into adulthood with no apparent alterations in gross brain morphology, but with defects in behavior and synaptic plasticity (Komiyama et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Komiyama et al., 2002.

claim: Syngap+/- neurons have, on average, larger spine heads.
source: Syngap+/- neurons have higher average numbers of AMPARs at their synapses than wt (Kim et al., 2003; Vazquez et al., 2004), and, have, on average, larger spine heads (Vazquez et al., 2004; Carlisle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and Carlisle et al., 2008.

claim: Syngap+/- neurons form excitatory synapses precociously in culture and during postnatal cortical and hippocampal development.
source: They form excitatory synapses precociously in culture (Vazquez et al., 2004) and also during postnatal cortical and hippocampal development (Clement et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and Clement et al., 2012.

claim: Precocious synapse formation in Syngap+/- neurons leads to an elevated E/I ratio (excitatory/inhibitory synaptic ratio) and derangement of critical developmental periods.
source: They form excitatory synapses precociously in culture (Vazquez et al., 2004) and also during postnatal cortical and hippocampal development (Clement et al., 2012), leading to an elevated E/I ratio (excitatory/inhibitory synaptic ratio) and derangement of critical developmental periods (Clement et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clement et al., 2013.

claim: The effect of overexpression of synGAP-α1 in cultured forebrain neurons on development of spines is rapid, measurable within 12–24 hr of transfection.
source: The effect of overexpression of synGAP-α1 in cultured forebrain neurons on development of spines (Vazquez et al., 2004) and on numbers of synaptic AMPARs (McMahon et al., 2012) is rapid, measurable within 12–24 hr of transfection and is not caused by mislocalization of the exogenous synGAP- α1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The effects of overexpression of synGAP-α1 are not dependent on the GAP activity of synGAP and they require the PDZ ligand.
source: These effects are predicted by our model and do not depend on the in vivo context of the neurons. They are also not dependent on the GAP activity of synGAP and they require the PDZ ligand.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: An increase in localization of neuroligin-2 at excitatory synapses is mediated by binding to PSD-95 and increases the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory synaptic contacts.
source: Several studies have shown that an increase in localization of neuroligin-2 at excitatory synapses is mediated by binding to PSD-95 and increases the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory synaptic contacts (Prange et al., 2004; Levinson et al., 2005; 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prange et al., 2004, Levinson et al., 2005, and Levinson et al., 2010.
